newsitem.title: USA: GM trades in historic headquarters for RenCen.
newsitem.headline: GM trades in historic headquarters for RenCen.

text.p: General Motors Corp., trading in 76 years of history for the promise of a more efficient future, Monday moved its top executives out of its landmark headquarters building to its new home in Detroit's Renaissance Center.

About 70 people, led by GM Chairman Jack Smith, and Vice Chairman Harry Pearce, became the first GM employees to move into the downtown glass-towered complex on the Detroit River, which will be called the General Motors Global Headquarters at The Renaissance Center.
GM bought the Renaissance Center, built in the 1970s with backing by the late Ford Motor Co. Chairman Henry Ford II, for about $72 million in May.

GM decided that the bargain-basement price was cheaper than the hundreds of millions of dollars it would have cost to renovate the neoclassical General Motors Building, which opened in 1920 in midtown Detroit.

Many GM veterans made careers out of trying to reach the building's plush 14th-floor executive suite, once considered the pinnacle of American corporate success. The structure gained unwelcome fame in the satirical film "Roger & Me" when producer Michael Moore was thrown out of its ornate lobby in his pursuit of an interview with then-GM Chairman Roger Smith.
But the building's antiquated wiring, lack of central air conditioning and traditional layout were no longer conducive to GM's modern, more efficient, management structure.

"This move represents much more than a change in location. It allows us an opportunity to redefine the way we work together as an organization," Smith said in a statement. "The layout of the (new) building provides opportunities for a collaborative work environment that simply are not available in a 'traditional' office environment of fixed walls and long corridors."

Some 9,000 GM employees from several Michigan cities will move into the 2.2 million-square-foot Renaissance Center gradually over the next five years, including the company's vehicle marketing divisions and support units.

Following the executive staff to the Renaissance Center will be the Pontiac/GMC marketing division, which will move approximately 400 employees about 30 miles from Pontiac, Mich., into seven floors of Tower 100 in the spring of 1997.

Plans for the four-tower facility's public areas call for a GM museum displaying historic cars and modern protoype vehicles and a state-of-the-art training and conference center where GM employees will come to upgrade their skills.
About 2,500 Ford marketing employees remain housed in the Renaissance Center, but Ford has not announced any plans to move prior to its lease expiration in 2005.

As for the 900,000-square-foot GM Building, designed by the famous industrial architect Albert Kahn to be the world's largest office building of its day, the automaker plans to deed it over to a private developer who will renovate it for use as Detroit's new City Hall and for other government-related tenants.

Separately, GM announced Monday that it is recalling about 49,000 1996-model Buick Skylark and Oldsmobile Achieva cars to repair an air bag-related defect. GM said its dealers will install a plastic protector that will prevent the possbility that the cars' passenger air bag could deploy behind the instrument panel instead of through a door in the panel.

GM also said strikes in the United States and Canada during October caused it to reduce its fourth-quarter North American production forecast by 151,000 units. The company now plans to build 1,169,000 cars and trucks in North America during the period, down about 14.8 percent from a year ago.
